NO-01-001: Stand at the Flydalsjuvet overlook high above Geiranger village and the fjord arm winds away beneath you, its dark water cutting between steep green mountainsides that fall to the shore. The stillness of late-September night settles over the valley, with the mountains fading into shadow layer upon layer. It is Norway's fjord country at its most quietly grand.
NO-01-002: Across Vågen bay, the Bryggen wharf rises as a row of gabled wooden houses, their painted facades shoulder to shoulder along the water. Bergen's old Hanseatic quarter glows softly under the late-night sky, masts and reflections shifting on the harbor below. The place has traded with the sea for centuries, and it shows.
NO-01-003: From the harbor promenade the Oslo Opera House lifts its white marble roof like a glacier calving into Oslofjord, and visitors climb its sloping planes for the view. Under the September night sky the building gleams pale against the dark water. It is the waterfront's most photographed silhouette.
NO-01-004: Step to the edge of the Preikestolen plateau and the granite slab juts squarely out over Lysefjorden, six hundred meters of air beneath your feet. The fjord stretches dark and narrow between the mountain walls under the late-night sky. Few ledges in Norway command quite this view.
NO-01-005: The curved wooden platform of Stegastein arcs out from the mountainside and puts you out over Aurlandsfjord with nothing between you and the drop. Fjord and mountains open beyond the timber rail, the water lying dark far below in the September night. A single look-out, and the whole valley at once.
NO-01-006: From the Reinebringen ridge trail the jagged Lofoten peaks rise on every side while the fishing village of Reine nestles at the fjord's edge below. Reinefjorden lies dark and still under the night sky, the scattered lights of the village winking across the water. Pure Lofoten drama.
NO-01-007: In the churchyard at Borgund the dark tarred stave church rises in tiered roofs, dragon heads jutting from the gables against the night sky. Carved details crowd every portal and pillar, black against the moonlit grass. Eight centuries of Norwegian timber craft in one building.
NO-01-008: From the roadside viewpoint the Storseisundet Bridge throws its dramatic curve out over the Atlantic, the carriageway arching where the ocean breaks below. Under the September night sky the span stands out as a sculptural sweep of concrete and steel. It is the Atlantic Road's famous calling card.
NO-01-009: Across the cathedral green, Nidaros Cathedral's great west front rises with its rows of carved statues standing in their niches. Norway's grandest Gothic church holds the night skyline of Trondheim, the stonework massed and quiet after dark. A thousand years of history in one facade.
NO-01-010: At the edge of the North Cape plateau the globe monument stands against the open Barents Sea, the cliff dropping sheer to the water. Under the late-September night the horizon runs dark and endless — Europe simply ends here. The wind and the sea do the talking.
NO-01-011: Norway's oldest stave church sits above Lustrafjorden at Urnes, its wooden shingles silvered by centuries and its carved portal weathered by time. From the churchyard the fjord opens below under the night sky, still and dark. A small building with an enormous past.
NO-01-012: From the plateau viewpoint the Trollstigen road drops away in eleven tight hairpins, the asphalt ribbon threading the mountainside with Stigfossen waterfall pouring beside it. Under the night sky the valley lies in shadow far below, the falls a white streak in the dark. Norway's most serpentine road.
NO-01-013: Along the Frogner Park axis the granite sculptures of Vigeland Park stand in long rows, and at the far end the Monolith rises as the park's unmistakable crown. In the September night the stone figures hold their poses in the dark, quiet and watchful. An open-air gallery like no other.
NO-01-014: Down the timbered street of Røros the old mining town lines up in weathered wooden houses, and above the rooftops the octagonal church crowns the hill. Under the night sky the street glows warm from its windows, snowless and still in late September. A working town that happens to be a museum.
NO-01-015: From the Tromsø side of the strait the Arctic Cathedral rises in its great triangular planes of glass and concrete, the sail-like form unmistakable against the September night. The glass gable catches the last of the light while the water lies dark below. A modern icon on the Tromsdalen shore.
NO-01-016: Step along the approach to Trolltunga and the rock ledge juts out horizontally, hanging over the dark waters of Ringedalsvatnet far below. The mountains ring the lake under the late-night sky, the ledge itself a thin tongue of granite in the dark. The photo every hiker comes for.
NO-01-017: Out on Geirangerfjord the Seven Sisters falls drop in a broad curtain down the cliff face, the water falling sheer into the fjord. Under the night sky the falls show pale against the dark rock, their mist drifting on the air. One of Norway's great waterfalls, best seen from the water.
NO-01-018: On the Dalsnibba Skywalk platform, fifteen hundred meters above Geirangerfjord, the glass floor lets you stand over the void while the fjord lies dark far below. The mountains fall away on all sides under the September night. Not a place for the faint-hearted — and not a view you forget.
NO-01-019: From the Fløyen terrace the whole of Bergen spreads below: the city and its harbor tucked between the hills, the fjord reaching out to sea. In the late-night dark the city lights trace the shoreline under the mountains. Bergen's classic panorama, worth the ride up.
NO-01-020: Above the harbor the Bergenhus Fortress holds its ground, the Rosenkrantz Tower and the medieval walls standing dark against the night sky. Bergen grew up in the shadow of these stones, and the old stronghold still watches the water. Eight centuries of defense in one view.
NO-01-021: Along the Bergen harbor the fish market stalls crowd the quay with boats bobbing at their moorings, the water of the harbor lapping the stone edge. Under the night sky the market glows at the heart of the old town. The smell of the sea is never far away.
NO-01-022: High above Oslofjord the ramparts of Akershus Fortress run along the ridge, the medieval walls standing dark over the water under the September night. The city lights spread below while the old fortress keeps its watch. Oslo's guardian since the 1300s.
NO-01-023: The Aker Brygge promenade runs modern and bright along the Oslofjord waterfront, its bars and boardwalks strung out above the dark water. Under the night sky the fjord lies quiet beyond the lights, with the city humming behind you. Oslo's evening front door.
NO-01-024: At the end of Karl Johans gate the Royal Palace stands with its gardens and parade ground spread below, the facade lit and formal under the September night. The city climbs toward it in a long straight line from the station. Norway's royal address, open and unguarded.
NO-01-025: The old harbor street of Stavanger lines up white wooden houses along the cobbles, their gables and fences leaning close over the lane. In the dark of the September night the little quarter glows softly, quiet behind its windows. Old Stavanger, beautifully kept.
NO-01-026: On the Hafrsfjord shore three enormous bronze swords stand planted in the rock, their blades rising against the night sky. The monument marks where Norway was gathered into one kingdom, and the shore lies still and dark around them. Simple, huge, and unforgettable.
NO-01-027: Through the steep Flåm valley the mountain railway winds its way, the track curving across bridges and beside waterfalls as it climbs from the fjord. In the dark of the night the valley walls close in, the train's line threading the blackness. One of the world's great railway rides.
NO-01-028: Tucked against the fjord, the tiny hamlet of Undredal clusters around Norway's smallest stave church, the dark wooden building small among the houses. Under the night sky the fjord lies still at the hamlet's feet, the mountains black above. A handful of houses and a jewel of a church.
NO-01-029: At the very tip of Lofoten the village of Å strings its red rorbu fishing cabins along the shore, the wooden cabins standing on stilts above the water. In the September night the fjord lies dark around them, the mountains looming behind. Lofoten's farthest outpost.
NO-01-030: Scattered across its skerries, Henningsvær gathers its fishing village around the harbor, with the island football pitch set flat among the rocks like a green tabletop. Under the night sky the village lights glitter on the water between the islands. A village with the most famous pitch in Norway.
NO-01-031: On the fjord shore the white wooden Kvernes stave church stands bright against the dark hillside, its pale walls catching the light under the September night. The water lies still at the church's feet, the mountains closing in behind. A quiet country church in a grand setting.
NO-01-032: Along the Nidelva river the colorful wooden houses of Bakklandet crowd the bank in reds, yellows and ochres, their gables reflected in the water. Under the night sky the old quarter glows warm from its windows. Trondheim's prettiest neighborhood, and its oldest.
NO-01-033: From the Kristiansten ramparts the fortress looks down over Trondheim and the fjord, the city spread below and the water dark beyond under the September night. The old stronghold has watched over the town for centuries, and the view explains why. The city at your feet.
NO-01-034: Beneath the North Cape plateau the little fishing hamlet of Skarsvåg huddles at the water's edge, its houses and boats gathered against the dark hillside. In the September night the hamlet glows small and warm under the great plateau. The world's northernmost fishing village.
NO-01-035: The Nigardsbreen glacier tongue descends toward its meltwater lake, the blue-white ice creased and furrowed where it calves into the dark water. Under the September night the glacier gleams pale against the black mountainside. An arm of the great Jostedalsbreen, close enough to touch.
NO-01-036: The Rampestreken platform juts out from the mountainside above Åndalsnes, putting you out over the void with Romsdalsfjord far below. In the night dark the fjord lies still and black, the mountains ringed in shadow. A steel balcony on the edge of the world.
NO-01-037: On the hillside above Røros the old copper mine works of Olavsgruva stand weathered and dark, the timbered buildings of the historic workings spread across the slope. Under the September night the industrial past of the town shows stark against the hills. Where Røros earned its living.
NO-01-038: From the Tromsø Bridge the great arch frames the Arctic Cathedral across the strait, the triangular glass gable rising on the far shore. Under the night sky the bridge's span and the cathedral make one of the Arctic's great compositions. Tromsø's two icons in a single frame.
NO-01-039: From the Fjellheisen summit the cable car has lifted you above Tromsø island, and the town lies below with the fjords reaching out dark on every side under the September night. The island's lights scatter across the water, the mountains black around them. The Arctic city from above.
NO-01-040: At Låtefossen the twin waterfall plunges down the rock face and pours beneath the old stone bridge, the water thundering under the arch. In the dark of the night the falls show white against the black cliff, their spray hanging in the air. A waterfall you drive right through.
NO-01-041: The Fiskebrygga boardwalk runs along the Kristiansand waterfront, its boats moored at the quay and the seafood stalls lined up above the water. Under the September night the harbor glows at the town's edge, the Skagerrak dark beyond. Kristiansand's lively water's edge.
NO-01-042: The seaside Christiansholm fortress faces the Skagerrak with its cannons trained on the water, the old round tower standing dark against the night sky. Kristiansand's harbor defenses have watched this approach for centuries. A small fortress with a commanding view.
NO-01-043: Bystranda beach curves along the Kristiansand shore, the promenade running behind it above the sand, the water of the bay stretching out under the soft light of dawn. In the early September morning the beach lies quiet and empty, the day not yet begun. The city's own stretch of summer.
NO-01-044: In the narrows of Oslofjord the island fortress of Oscarsborg guards the channel, its old walls and batteries standing dark against the water under the September night. The fjord squeezes past on either side — the whole of Oslo once depended on this rock. History at the waterline.
NO-01-045: Along the fjord shore at Drøbak the old wooden houses crowd down to the water with boats at their moorings, the little town strung out along the quay. In the first light of dawn the harbor glows softly, the fjord lying calm beyond. A fjord town waking up.
NO-01-046: Eidsvoll Manor stands in its park with the white main house and its outbuildings arranged around the courtyard, the place where Norway's constitution was signed. In the soft morning light the manor's facade gleams against the green grounds. The birthplace of modern Norway.
NO-01-047: The baroque church of Kongsberg rises above the old mining town, its great tower and pale facade dominating the rooftops under the September morning sky. The town of the silver mines built this church to show its wealth, and it still does. Kongsberg's crown.
NO-01-048: Along the Numedalslågen the old mining town of Kongsberg strings its wooden houses and works along the river, the water running dark and quick under the morning light. The river powered the mines that built the town, and it still runs through its heart. Industry and water, side by side.
NO-01-049: The Drammen Spiral tunnels up through the rock in a great corkscrew, emerging at the Skansen viewpoint high above the town. In the morning light the city and the Drammensfjord open below, the water bright in the valley. A road through the mountain for the sake of the view.
NO-01-050: Above Lake Mjøsa the Maihaugen open-air museum spreads its old farmsteads across the hillside, the timbered houses and barns gathered as a village out of time. In the September morning light the lake gleams below, the mountains beyond. Norwegian country life, preserved whole.
NO-01-051: The Lysgårdsbakkene ski jumps tower over Lillehammer, the great inruns and scaffolding standing stark against the morning sky. From their feet the town lies below and Lake Mjøsa beyond, the Olympic hills quiet in September. The jumps that carried the 1994 Games.
NO-01-052: At Domkirkeodden the medieval cathedral ruins stand sheltered under their great glass canopy, the old stone arches preserved against the weather by Mjøsa's shore. In the soft morning light the glass gleams and the ruins show dark beneath it. Hamar's ancient cathedral, kept for the future.
NO-01-053: From the summit of Gaustatoppen the panorama opens across Telemark, the mountain ridges rolling away under the September morning sky with the hardanger plateau beyond. On a clear day a sixth of Norway lies in view from this one top. Telemark's landmark mountain earns its fame.
NO-01-054: Beneath the Rjukan waterfall the Vemork heavy water plant clings to the gorge, the industrial buildings of the old works strung along the cliff under the morning light. The falls thunder above the plant that made wartime history. A quiet valley with a loud past.
NO-01-055: The historic locks of the Telemark Canal lift boats between Skien and Dalen, the old stone chambers and gates stepping up through the green valley. In the soft morning light the water lies still in the lock basins, the hills rising on either side. Norway's canal, hand-built and still working.
NO-01-056: The castle hill of Slottsfjellet rises above Tønsberg with its tower standing against the morning sky, the town spread below toward the fjord. Norway's oldest town grew up in this hill's shadow, and the tower still marks the spot. The view that watched a thousand years of history.
NO-01-057: The Oseberg mound rises green and grassy in the rolling Tønsberg farmland, the great Viking burial mound smooth against the morning sky. Beneath it the famous ship once lay, and the field around keeps its quiet. A king's grave in an ordinary meadow.
NO-01-058: The beech forest of Bøkeskogen climbs the hill above Larvik, its paths winding through tall smooth trunks under the soft morning light. Norway's largest beech wood stands cool and green above the town, the leaves turning early in September. A forest walk with a view at the top.
NO-01-059: The fortified old town of Gamlebyen stands behind its moats and ramparts at Fredrikstad, the old earthen walls and gates enclosing the grid of wooden houses. In the morning light the fortifications show green and calm, the water in the moats still. Norway's best-kept fortress town.
NO-01-060: Along the Glomma the Fredrikstad waterfront lines up old warehouses and bridges, the broad river running past the quays under the September morning light. Boats lie at their moorings and the town's industrial past shows along the banks. The river that built the town.
NO-01-061: The Fredriksten fortress walls run along the ridge above Halden, the old bastions and gates looking out over the Iddefjord and the border country. In the morning light the ramparts stand weathered and proud above the town. The fortress Sweden never took.
NO-01-062: On the rock above Altafjord the ancient carvings of Alta lie etched in the stone, the UNESCO panels showing reindeer and hunters in the morning light. The red-painted figures stand out against the grey rock, five thousand years old and still speaking. The Arctic's oldest picture book.
NO-01-063: The Northern Lights Cathedral spirals up from the Alta town center, its titanium-clad form twisting toward the morning sky like a flame. The metal skin catches the light and the strange, beautiful building dominates the street. A cathedral built for the aurora, shining by day too.
NO-01-064: The Hammerfest harbor stretches along the Arctic waterfront, the town's houses and quays gathered around the water with the Meridian column standing by the shore. In the September morning the harbor lies calm under the pale northern light. The world's northernmost town, going about its day.
NO-01-065: Beneath the bridge at Saltstraumen the tidal current boils and swirls, the maelstrom churning white where the strait squeezes the tide. In the morning light the whirlpools show dark and foaming under the span. The world's strongest tidal current, best watched from the bridge.
NO-01-066: The Bodø harbor promenade runs along the Vestfjorden waterfront, the town's new quarter bright against the water under the late-September morning sun. Boats cross the fjord beyond the quay while the mountains stand across the water. Nordland's capital, facing the sea.
NO-01-067: From the Narvikfjellet cable car the view opens over Ofotfjorden and the town, the water running dark between the mountains under the morning light. Narvik lies below at the fjord's head, the peaks rising on every side. The Ofoten line's mountain panorama.
NO-01-068: The 13th-century Heddal stave church stands in its rural setting, the great triple-naved wooden church rising dark and carved against the morning sky. Norway's largest stave church holds the valley with its dragon heads and shingled roofs. Eight hundred years of timber, still standing.
NO-01-069: The historic manor park of Brekkeparken spreads its grounds above Skien, the old farm buildings and gardens of the open-air museum arranged across the green hillside. In the soft morning light the town lies below and the park keeps its calm. Old Telemark, preserved above the town.
NO-01-070: On the shore of Lake Bandak the Dalen Hotel rises in dragon style, the 19th-century wooden hotel ornate with carved gables and towers under the morning sun. The great white-and-timber building stands like a stave church turned hotel at the water's edge. Norway's fairytale hotel.
NO-01-071: Beside the Vest-Telemark museum the medieval Eidsborg stave church stands small and dark, its shingled roofs and carved details weathered by centuries. In the morning light the little church shows its age proudly against the green museum grounds. One of Telemark's oldest treasures.
NO-01-072: The Venstøp farm museum keeps Henrik Ibsen's childhood home, the old farmhouse and outbuildings gathered in their rural setting outside Skien. In the soft morning light the yard lies quiet, the buildings weathered and honest. Where Norway's greatest playwright grew up.
NO-01-073: Seljordsvatnet stretches long and still with the village on its shore, the lake of the Selma sea-serpent legend lying calm under the late-September morning sun. The mountains rise around the water and the village keeps its watch on the deep. Keep an eye out for Selma.
NO-01-074: The resort village of Vrådal lies along the shore of Lake Nisser, its cabins and boathouses scattered above the water under the morning sun. The lake stretches out dark and calm between the Telemark hills, the village quiet in September. A lakeside pause in the high country.
NO-01-075: From the high road above Rauland, the mountain village spreads across the valley floor — scattered farmsteads and timber cabins ringed by low birch woods, with bare rounded fells rising behind in the late-September morning light. The first autumn colors touch the highland slopes, and the whole settlement feels tucked deep into the Telemark highlands. A quiet, sturdy piece of Norway, wide open to the sky.
NO-01-076: The old stone church of Kviteseidbyen stands solid in the heart of the canal village, its weathered walls glowing in the midday sun. Around it the white wooden houses of the village gather along the water of the Telemark Canal. It is one of those places where history feels close enough to touch.
NO-01-077: Set in the rolling Telemark countryside, Bø Sommarland spreads its pools and slides across a green hillside under the late-morning sun. The water park's bright attractions stand out against the farmland and forest around it. One of Norway's best-loved summer days out — and even in September the place holds its cheerful promise.
NO-01-078: Beneath the high fells of Hjartdal, the mountain village of Tuddal lies scattered along the valley, farmhouses and cabins among autumn-colored birch. The great fell tops rise all around in the midday light, already hinting at the coming snow season. A working mountain community at the foot of some of Telemark's grandest heights.
NO-01-079: Åmdals Verk keeps the look of its copper-mining past — historic timber buildings grouped in the Tokke hills, surrounded by forest under the September midday sun. The settlement tells the story of the miners who once worked these hills, the old works buildings standing as quiet monuments. Industrial heritage set deep in Telemark's wooded country.
NO-01-080: From the rocky point at Lindesnes, Norway's southernmost tip, the white lighthouse tower with its red top rises center-frame above the low heathland. Waves break on the rocks at its base while the open sea stretches to the horizon under the midday sun. Standing here at the very edge of the country, the meeting of Skagerrak and North Sea feels raw and elemental.
NO-01-081: Walking the curve of Sjøsanden's pale sand, the beach sweeps around the bay with calm water and small boats mid-frame. Low granite skerries dot the offshore water, and pine-covered slopes rise behind the beach in the midday light. Mandal's own Riviera — a sheltered, sun-warmed corner of the south coast.
NO-01-082: From the Pollen quay, the sheltered harbor basin lies before you — small boats moored along wooden piers, white and pastel wooden houses lining both sides of the inlet, and the town church rising above the rooftops in the early-afternoon sun. This is the classic sørlandet harbor town, proud of its seafaring past and polished for visitors.
NO-01-083: Along the harbor promenade at Grimstad, fishing boats and leisure craft crowd the quays while the white wooden houses of the old town face the water. The harbor opens toward the skerries offshore, glowing in the afternoon light. A town that has lived by the sea for centuries — and still does.
NO-01-084: From the Lillesand harbor front, the white wooden town houses line the quay behind the marina, and the sheltered Blindleia strait threads past low granite skerries dotted with cabins beyond. In the afternoon sun this protected waterway shows why boaters call it one of Norway's finest passages. Shelter, calm water, and the south coast at its gentlest.
NO-01-085: From the harbor quay, rows of white-painted wooden houses climb the hillside around the inlet, masts of moored boats in the foreground and the church on the rise above the town. Risør glows in the afternoon light — the wooden boat town, kept bright and shipshape as it has been for generations.
NO-01-086: Across the harbor inlet, wooden boathouses and small boats line the quays while white wooden town houses with their shops face the water, forested slopes framing the far side of the inlet in the afternoon sun. The book town of the south coast, wrapped around its quiet harbor.
NO-01-087: From the fjord-side promenade, the row of white wooden houses with their distinctive gables faces the water, boats at the town quays and steep hills rising directly behind the settlement in the afternoon light. The old Dutch Quarter keeps its 18th-century trading-post character, proud and well kept.
NO-01-088: From the village jetty, white wooden fishing houses cluster around the small harbor, working boats moored alongside, with skerries and open sea beyond the harbor mouth under the afternoon sun. Loshavn is the south coast's best-preserved fishing village — salt-weathered, authentic, and still tied to the sea.
NO-01-089: Along the sandy shoreline of the Rosfjord, pale sand and shallow water fill the foreground while the narrow fjord extends inland between forested hills, a few cabins along the far shore in the afternoon light. A quiet fjord beach, made for slow September afternoons.
NO-01-090: From the hillside road above Knaben, the former mining village spreads across the valley floor — low historic mine buildings and cabins set among heathland, with rounded mountain tops framing the settlement in the afternoon sun. The molybdenum mines are history now, but the high mountain village keeps its rugged character.
NO-01-091: Across the mountain village in upper Setesdal, scattered cabins and lodges sit among low birch and heather, with bare rounded peaks rising on all sides of the valley floor in the afternoon light. Hovden in September wears its autumn colors openly — a mountain resort resting between seasons.
NO-01-092: Across the park's open-air grounds, mineral exhibits and historic mine-era buildings sit among pines on the hillside, with the Otra river valley and its forested slopes falling away beyond in the afternoon sun. A place where Norway's mineral wealth is on proud display, set in lovely Setesdal scenery.
NO-01-093: Above the valley, the ski mountainside carries lift lines and marked pistes down the fell toward the base-area buildings, with the Sirdal valley and its lakes spreading out below in the afternoon light. In September the slopes lie quiet and green, waiting for the snow that made this mountain famous.
NO-01-094: From the town square, the timber-clad library and culture house presents its curved wooden rib structure through the glass front, with the plaza and surrounding town-center buildings completing the frame in the afternoon sun. A modern landmark of Norwegian timber architecture, right in the heart of Vennesla.
NO-01-095: From the Drøbak harbour side, the view crosses the sound toward the fortress islands — wooded Kaholmene slopes to the left, the white fortress buildings and gun batteries of Søndre Kaholmen in the center, and the Oslofjord narrows opening to the right, with ferries crossing in the foreground under the afternoon sun. The fortress that stopped the Blücher, standing guard over the fjord.
NO-01-096: From the garden in front of the manor, the lawn sweeps past old trees to the ochre-yellow wooden manor with its white columns and main entrance facing the viewer, the flagpole and garden beds framing it against birch and pine woodland in the afternoon sun. The birthplace of Norway's constitution — Eidsvollsbygningen, dignified and welcoming.
NO-01-097: Standing on Storgata by the harbour, the row of low white-and-ochre timber houses lines the waterfront street to the left, the harbour with its moored boats and small customs-house pier fills the center, and the Oslofjord stretches to the right toward the Kaholmene islands, Oscarsborg's white buildings visible across the water. Drøbak keeps its old coastal-town charm at every step.
NO-01-098: On Storgata looking toward the fjord, the historic timber warehouses and merchants' houses of the old trading town stand to the left, the street slopes down to the small harbour in the center with the Oslofjord beyond, and the marina with its sailboats fills the right, the low green hills of Vestby rising behind. Son wears its seafaring past handsomely.
NO-01-099: On Verksgata in the historic ironworks village, the preserved low timber workshops and smithies line the Lomma river to the left, the cobbled street of craft shops and galleries runs through the center, and restored foundry-era buildings with tarred-timber facades stand to the right against the wooded hillside. A 17th-century ironworks turned into one of Norway's most atmospheric craft villages.
NO-01-100: On the floating walkway through the timber-boom park, the still black water of the Glomma delta with its wooden sorting channels lies to the left, the historic timber structures and winch towers of the lenser stand center, and reed beds with the broad water of Øyeren stretch to the right toward the forested shoreline. A working monument to Norway's timber-floating age, set in a thriving river delta.
NO-01-101: From the open lawn of the university park, avenues of mature broadleaf trees and flowering plantings stretch to the left, the lawn rolls toward the red-brick historic main buildings of the Norwegian University of Life Sciences in the center, and the pond with sculptural plantings fills the right, the fields of Ås beyond. One of Norway's loveliest campuses — part park, part botanical showcase.
NO-01-102: On the lakeside trail at the eastern shore, the calm lake water mirrors the surrounding woodland to the left, Semsvannet's open surface bordered by reed beds and the gravel walking path fills the center, and the slopes of Skaugumsåsen rise to the right above the nature reserve's treeline. A protected natural gem, minutes from Asker's streets.
NO-01-103: In the old town center of Hølen, the protected timber houses of the small kjøpstad line the narrow street to the left, old shop fronts and the white church gable stand center, and the Såna river valley with its fields and the wooded ridges of Vestby opens to the right. A pocket of preserved small-town Norway, quiet and unhurried.
NO-01-104: From the Strømsø riverbank, the cable-stayed Ypsilon footbridge arcs across the Drammenselva, its harp-like cables and Y-shaped pylon at center frame, the river and city waterfront completing the view in the late-afternoon light. Drammen's most photographed structure — a piece of modern engineering that has become a city landmark.
NO-01-105: Across the Marienlyst park lawns, the white manor house of the Drammens Museum stands center frame with its heritage garden around it, the open-air museum's timber buildings and old trees framing the grounds in the late-afternoon sun. Art, history, and a fine old park in one visit.
NO-01-106: In the museum courtyard, the historic smelting-works buildings of the Norwegian Mining Museum stand in warm timber and stone, the old works chimney and courtyard completing the industrial-heritage frame under the late-afternoon sun. Kongsberg's silver-mining story, told where it happened.
NO-01-107: Across the cobbled works yard, the blue-painted cobalt works buildings of Blaafarveværket stand out with their white trim, old industrial buildings and surrounding birch woodland completing the frame in the late-afternoon light. Once the world's largest cobalt works — now a celebrated arts and heritage site.
NO-01-108: From the bridge above the falls, the Hønefossen waterfall pours through the town center below, the Begna river, the old Hønefoss bridge and town buildings completing the frame in the late-afternoon light. A waterfall right in the middle of town — Hønefoss wears its namesake with pride.

One of Hallingdal's oldest churches, rich with medieval painted decoration inside.
